title: What a guesstimate is and how it is judged
blurb: A guesstimate is structured reasoning to a defensible number, not a hunt for the exact answer.

lessons.heading: It is about the path, not the number
lessons.body: Nobody expects you to know how many chai cups Mumbai drinks a day. The interviewer watches how you break the problem down, which assumptions you pick and whether the result is sensible. A clean structure with a slightly wrong number beats a lucky number with no logic.

lessons.heading: What interviewers score
lessons.body: Typical scoring covers four things: structure, reasonable assumptions, comfortable arithmetic and a sanity check. Being within a factor of 2 to 3 of the real answer is usually fine. Being off by a factor of 100 (say, ₹10 lakh instead of ₹10 crore) signals a broken model.

lessons.heading: State your approach first
lessons.body: Before any numbers, say in one line how you will attack it: 'I will start from the population of Pune, split into households, and estimate how many buy a scooter.' This gives the interviewer a map and lets them redirect you early. It also stops you from wandering.

lessons.heading: Think aloud and write it down
lessons.body: Silence looks like being stuck. Speak each assumption as you make it and note it on a page in a tidy tree or table. A written structure also protects you if you lose track of a number mid-way.

lessons.heading: Always finish with one number
lessons.body: End with a clear sentence: 'So roughly 50 lakh cups per day in Mumbai.' Add a one-line sanity check and, if asked, the biggest lever on your answer. A guesstimate with no conclusion feels unfinished.

example.prompt: How many cups of chai are sold outside homes in Mumbai in a day?
walk: Approach: population, then adults who buy chai outside, then cups each.
Mumbai city is about 1.3 crore people.
Adults are about 70%, so ~90 lakh adults.
Say 40% buy chai outside on a given day: ~36 lakh people.
Each has about 1.5 cups: 36 lakh x 1.5 = 54 lakh.
Round: about 50 lakh cups a day.
Sanity: that is roughly 1 cup per 2.5 residents, plausible for a tea-loving city.

quiz.q: Which set best describes what interviewers score in a guesstimate?
options: Closeness to the true figure, speed of calculation and use of recent industry data
Depth of market knowledge, accuracy of the final figure and confident delivery
Structure, sensible assumptions, comfortable arithmetic and a final sanity check
Number of assumptions listed, precision of decimals and finishing within five minutes
quiz.why: Interviewers reward a clear path, reasonable inputs, easy arithmetic and a check. The tempting 'closeness to the true figure' misses that being within 2x to 3x is fine and logic matters more than luck.

quiz.q: You get ₹10 lakh, but a quick check suggests the answer should be near ₹10 crore. What does this tell you?
options: The model has a 100x error, so recheck units and each step for a slip
The answer is in a normal range because lakh and crore are close in size
The gap is roughly 10x, so a small tweak to one assumption will fix it
The check is unreliable, so keep the first answer since the logic looked clean
quiz.why: 1 crore is 100 lakh, so ₹10 lakh versus ₹10 crore is a 100x gap, which signals a broken model. Treating it as a 10x gap makes it sound like a minor tweak.

quiz.q: The interviewer finishes reading the question. What is the best first move?
options: Start with the population figure and begin multiplying while thinking silently
Ask for the real industry data so your inputs are accurate from the start
Pick the most precise numbers you know and build the answer around them
State your approach in one line so the interviewer can redirect you early
quiz.why: A one-line map of your approach lets the interviewer steer you and keeps you from wandering. Asking for real data is tempting, but guesstimates test your own assumptions.

quiz.q: Which closing is best after estimating chai cups sold in Mumbai?
options: That gives 54.0 lakh cups a day, which I am confident matches the real figure
So roughly 50 lakh cups a day, which is about one cup for every 2.5 residents
My assumptions could be off, so the answer may be anywhere from 10 to 100 lakh
I have shown every step above, so that is my answer for you to judge
quiz.why: A strong close gives one rounded number plus a sanity check. The decimal-precise option sounds exact but claims accuracy your rough inputs cannot support.

title: Clarify and structure before you calculate
blurb: Two minutes of scoping saves ten minutes of rework.

lessons.heading: Pin down the question
lessons.body: Ask what exactly is being counted and over what period. 'Food delivery in Bengaluru' could mean orders, rupees, riders or restaurants. Confirm the geography (city limits or metro area), the time frame (per day, per year) and the unit (₹, units, people).

lessons.heading: Define the boundaries
lessons.body: Decide what is in and out. Do you include Swiggy-style apps only, or also phone-in orders and dabba services? Say your choice aloud and keep it fixed. Changing the definition halfway makes your numbers inconsistent.

lessons.heading: Choose the approach, then draw the tree
lessons.body: After clarifying, say which approach fits: top-down from population, bottom-up from a unit, or from supply capacity. Sketch a short tree with 3 to 5 boxes that multiply to the answer. Fewer boxes means fewer errors.

lessons.heading: Clarify the goal, not just the words
lessons.body: Ask why the number is needed. If it is for opening a store, the target is local demand, not national. If it is for a rough market size, a 2x range is fine. This tells you how much precision to chase.

lessons.heading: Do not over-ask
lessons.body: Two to four sharp questions is enough. Interviewers get impatient if you ask for data they cannot give. When they say 'assume what you think is reasonable', do so and speak your assumption clearly.

example.prompt: How many food delivery orders are placed in Bengaluru in a day?
walk: Clarify: app orders only, within the city, per day, counted in orders.
Approach: households, share that use apps, orders per user per week.
Bengaluru has ~1.4 crore people, ~35 lakh households.
Assume 30% use delivery apps: ~10 lakh households.
Each orders ~2 times a week: 20 lakh orders a week.
Per day: 20 lakh / 7 = ~3 lakh orders.
Sanity: 3 lakh orders over ~12 active hours is about 25,000 an hour, plausible.

quiz.q: The prompt says 'estimate the market for water bottles in Delhi'. Which clarification adds the most value?
options: Ask which brand of bottle is most popular so you can anchor on one big player
Confirm the unit, the time period and whether only packaged water counts
Ask for the exact population of Delhi so that your base number is accurate
Ask how the interviewer would estimate it so you can follow their chosen method
quiz.why: Unit, period and scope decide what you are counting. Asking for the population feels useful but is an input you can assume yourself.

quiz.q: Midway you realise you counted app orders but then added phone-in restaurant orders. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since counting more orders only makes the estimate more complete
You should have chosen a bottom-up method instead of a top-down method here
Your population base is too large, so the filters need to be tightened further
You changed the definition midway, so the earlier numbers no longer match
quiz.why: Boundaries must be fixed once stated, otherwise inputs describe different things. Adding more orders seems harmless but makes the numbers inconsistent.

quiz.q: Which tree is best for 'number of scooters bought per year in Pune'?
options: Pune households x share buying a scooter yearly x scooters per buyer
Number of showrooms x staff per showroom x scooters sold per staff in a day
Pune population x share who ride scooters x average scooter price in ₹
Pune households x share owning a scooter x years each owner keeps it
quiz.why: The correct tree multiplies to scooters per year. The showroom tree ends in a daily figure and the price tree ends in ₹, so the unit or period is wrong.

quiz.q: The interviewer says 'assume whatever you think is reasonable'. What do you do?
options: Ask again until the interviewer gives you a specific number to use
Choose conservative values so the answer cannot be called too high
State each assumption aloud, pick a sensible value and carry on
Pick reasonable values quietly so the flow is not interrupted
quiz.why: Saying assumptions aloud lets the interviewer follow and correct you. Quietly picking values hides your logic, and pressing for numbers wastes time on data they cannot give.

title: Top-down estimation
blurb: Start from a big known number and carve it down with percentages.

lessons.heading: What top-down means
lessons.body: You begin with a large, well-known base such as India's ~145 crore people or ~30 crore households. Then you apply filters (urban share, income, usage) until you reach your target group. It is fast and good for market-size questions.

lessons.heading: Pick the right base
lessons.body: Choose the base closest to the buyer. For toothpaste, households or individuals; for scooters, urban households with a middle income. A base that is too broad forces many noisy filters.

lessons.heading: Use clean percentages and ratios
lessons.body: Say '1 in 4 households' or '30%' rather than 27.3%. Ratios like 1 in 6 are easy to multiply with lakh and crore numbers. Keep each filter independent so you do not double-filter the same group.

lessons.heading: Watch for compounding error
lessons.body: Each filter has uncertainty, and they multiply. Four filters each off by 20% can leave you far from the truth. Use fewer filters and make the biggest one your most careful assumption.

lessons.heading: Convert to the asked unit at the end
lessons.body: If you counted households but the question wants ₹, multiply by a price at the final step. Write the unit next to each number. This avoids the classic mix of people and households.

example.prompt: What is the annual toothpaste market in India in ₹?
walk: Approach: households x usage x spend per household.
India has ~30 crore households.
Assume 90% use toothpaste: ~27 crore households.
A household buys about 8 tubes a year.
At ~₹80 a tube, that is about ₹640 per household.
27 crore x ₹640 = about ₹17,300 crore.
Round: roughly ₹17,000 crore a year. Sanity: ~₹120 per person per year, plausible.

quiz.q: Which base is best for 'annual sales of school bags in India'?
options: India's school-going children, since each bag is bought for one child
India's total population of ~145 crore, then filter down to the age group
All ~30 crore households, then filter by income and school enrolment
Number of schools in India, then multiply by bags needed per school
quiz.why: Pick the base closest to the buyer. Total population or households also work in theory but need more noisy filters to reach the target group.

quiz.q: You compute 30 crore households x 90% x 50% x 40% x 30% x 60%. What is the main concern?
options: The percentages are not round enough, so the product will be imprecise
The order of the filters is wrong, since the largest should come last
Five filters compound their error, so use fewer and be careful with the biggest
The base of 30 crore households is too small to give a usable answer
quiz.why: Each filter carries error and the errors multiply, so fewer filters is safer. Filter order does not change a product, which is the trap in the second option.

quiz.q: 27 crore households buy 8 tubes a year at ₹80 each. Which total is correct?
options: About ₹1,730 crore
About ₹17,300 crore
About ₹1.7 lakh crore
About ₹2,400 crore
quiz.why: 8 x ₹80 = ₹640 per household, and 27 crore x 640 is about ₹17,300 crore. The 10x errors come from slipping a zero, and adding 8 and 80 gives the ₹2,400 crore trap.

quiz.q: Which line shows poor top-down hygiene?
options: Take 30 crore households, keep the 90% who use toothpaste, then apply price
Say 1 in 4 households own a car, then apply that to 30 crore households
Count households first, then multiply by a price at the last step in ₹
Take 145 crore people, keep 30%, then multiply by spend per household
quiz.why: The flawed line starts with people but ends with a per-household figure, the classic people versus households mix. The other lines keep units consistent and use clean ratios.

title: Bottom-up estimation
blurb: Build the total from one real unit, such as a shop, a stall or a household.

lessons.heading: What bottom-up means
lessons.body: You start from one small unit you can picture, such as a chai stall, and estimate how much it does. Then you multiply by how many such units exist. It feels more concrete than top-down, so it is great when you can visualise the unit.

lessons.heading: Build a day in the life
lessons.body: Walk through one unit's day: opening hours, customers per hour, price per sale. Rush hours versus slow hours matter, so split them if needed. Your numbers should feel like something you have actually seen on a street in Chennai or Jaipur.

lessons.heading: Scale carefully
lessons.body: The hard part is how many such units exist. Use density: one stall per X thousand people, or per lane. Remember not all units are equal, so separate big and small ones.

lessons.heading: Mind operating days and capacity
lessons.body: A shop is not open 365 days at peak. Use ~300 working days for a typical small business and cap throughput by capacity: seats, burners, staff hours. Capacity limits protect you from impossible numbers.

lessons.heading: Cross-check against top-down
lessons.body: When time permits, check your bottom-up with a quick top-down. If one says ₹500 crore and the other ₹5,000 crore, find which assumption is off. Agreement within a factor of 2 builds confidence.

example.prompt: Estimate the monthly revenue of a busy idli-dosa stall in Chennai.
walk: Approach: customers per hour x hours x ticket size x days.
Peak hours are 6 to 11 am: 5 hours.
About 40 customers per hour at peak: 200 customers.
Add slow hours: ~50 more customers. Total ~250 a day.
Average bill ~₹50: 250 x 50 = ₹12,500 a day.
Open 26 days a month: about ₹3.25 lakh.
Round: ~₹3 lakh a month. Sanity: with 35 percent margin that is ~₹1 lakh profit, plausible for a good stall.

quiz.q: Which question suits a bottom-up approach best?
options: Estimating total smartphone sales across all of India in the coming year
Estimating how many people in India buy health insurance in a year
Estimating national spend on school uniforms across all the states
Estimating monthly revenue of one busy tyre-repair shop in Jaipur
quiz.why: Bottom-up works when you can picture a single unit and its day. National market questions with no obvious unit are easier from a large population base.

quiz.q: A stall serves 40 customers an hour for 12 hours. What is the likely flaw?
options: Twelve hours is too short, since most stalls stay open all day
It applies peak footfall to every hour, ignoring slow periods
Forty customers an hour is too low for a stall in any Indian city
It skips competing stalls, so demand per stall is overstated
quiz.why: A day-in-the-life estimate should split rush and slow hours. Competition matters when scaling, but the direct error here is applying the peak rate throughout.

quiz.q: A stall serves 250 customers a day at ₹50 and is open 26 days a month. What is monthly revenue?
options: About ₹32.5 lakh
About ₹3.9 lakh
About ₹3.25 lakh
About ₹12,500
quiz.why: 250 x 50 = ₹12,500 a day, and x 26 gives about ₹3.25 lakh. ₹12,500 forgets the days, and ₹32.5 lakh is a slipped zero.

quiz.q: When scaling one stall up to a whole city, which input is usually the biggest lever?
options: How many such stalls exist, such as stalls per thousand people
The average bill per customer, since prices differ between stalls
The number of working days per month, which is hard to pin down
Opening hours per stall, because they set how long each one runs
quiz.why: The hard part of bottom-up is the count of units, and it multiplies the whole answer. Price, days and hours vary only within a narrow range.

title: Rounding and mental math with lakh and crore
blurb: Convert units without slipping and keep arithmetic light.

lessons.heading: Know the Indian units cold
lessons.body: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 = 10^5. 1 crore = 100 lakh = 10^7. 1 lakh crore = 10^12. Also 1 million = 10 lakh and 1 billion = 100 crore. Most mistakes in interviews are unit slips, so drill these.

lessons.heading: Count zeros, not digits
lessons.body: Write numbers as a base times a power of ten. 2.5 lakh x 40 thousand = 2.5 x 10^5 x 4 x 10^4 = 10 x 10^9 = 10^10, which is 1,000 crore. Multiply the small parts, add the exponents.

lessons.heading: Round to friendly numbers
lessons.body: Turn 149 into 150 and 1.37 crore into 1.4 crore. Round up one number and down another so errors cancel. Choose numbers that multiply easily, like 4, 5, 25 and 50.

lessons.heading: Do not chase decimals
lessons.body: Two significant figures are plenty. Saying 5.4372 lakh sounds precise but is not, given your inputs are rough. Quote the final answer as 'roughly 5 lakh'.

lessons.heading: Use shortcuts
lessons.body: Dividing by 5 is multiplying by 2 and dividing by 10. Multiplying by 25 is dividing by 4 and multiplying by 100. For percentages, find 10% first and scale. Practise speaking the steps while you do them.

example.prompt: A streaming app has 3.2 crore paying users at ₹149 a month. What is annual revenue?
walk: Round ₹149 to ₹150 and 3.2 crore stays.
Monthly: 3.2 crore x 150 = 480 crore.
3.2 x 15 = 48, then crore x 10 gives 480 crore.
Annual: 480 crore x 12 = 5,760 crore.
Round: about ₹5,800 crore.
In lakh crore terms that is about 0.06 lakh crore.
Check: 3.2 crore users x ₹1,800 a year = ~₹5,800 crore.

quiz.q: What is 2.5 lakh x 40 thousand?
options: About 100 crore
About 10 crore
About 1,000 crore
About 10,000 crore
quiz.why: 2.5 x 10^5 x 4 x 10^4 = 10 x 10^9 = 10^10, and 1 crore is 10^7, so that is 1,000 crore. Miscounting a zero gives the 100 or 10,000 crore options.

quiz.q: 1 billion equals how many crore?
options: Equal to 100 crore
Equal to 10 crore
Equal to 1,000 crore
Equal to 10 lakh
quiz.why: 1 billion is 10^9 and 1 crore is 10^7, so it is 100 crore. 10 lakh is 1 million, which is the common mix-up.

quiz.q: 50 lakh households spend ₹1,200 a month each. What is annual spend?
options: About ₹720 crore
About ₹600 crore
About ₹72,000 crore
About ₹7,200 crore
quiz.why: 50 lakh x ₹1,200 is ₹600 crore a month, and x 12 gives about ₹7,200 crore. ₹600 crore forgets the 12 months, and the others slip a zero.

quiz.q: Which rounding habit is best?
options: Round every number up so the final answer stays on the safe side
Round one number up and another down so the errors partly cancel
Keep four or five decimals so rounding never distorts the result
Round only the final answer and keep every input exact until then
quiz.why: Offsetting up and down roundings keeps the product near the truth. Rounding everything the same way compounds the error, and extra decimals add false precision.

title: Segmentation and MECE
blurb: Split the population into groups that do not overlap and leave nothing out.

lessons.heading: MECE in plain words
lessons.body: Mutually exclusive means no person sits in two buckets. Collectively exhaustive means every person sits in some bucket. Splitting Indians into 'urban' and 'rural' is MECE; splitting into 'students' and 'young people' is not.

lessons.heading: Pick the cut that changes behaviour
lessons.body: Segment by the factor that really changes the number: income for smartphones, age for school fees, city tier for cars. A cut that does not change behaviour only adds work. Ask yourself, would these groups give different answers?

lessons.heading: Keep it to 3 or 4 segments
lessons.body: Low, middle and high income is usually enough. More segments mean more guesses and more room for slips. Make shares add up to 100% and say so aloud.

lessons.heading: Spot double counting
lessons.body: Counting a family's scooter once for the husband and again for the wife is double counting. So is counting both 'working women' and 'all women' in one sum. Check each unit is counted exactly once.

lessons.heading: Give each segment its own number
lessons.body: Each bucket gets its own size and its own usage or price. A rich household may spend ₹600 a month on mobile and a lower-income one ₹200. Add the segment totals at the end.

example.prompt: Monthly mobile recharge spend in a city of 50 lakh people.
walk: Phone users: 50 lakh x 80% = 40 lakh.
Segment by income: low 40%, middle 45%, high 15%.
Low: 16 lakh users x ₹200 = 32 crore.
Middle: 18 lakh users x ₹350 = 63 crore.
High: 6 lakh users x ₹600 = 36 crore.
Shares sum to 100%, users sum to 40 lakh.
Total: 32 + 63 + 36 = 131 crore, about ₹130 crore a month. Sanity: ₹130 crore / 40 lakh users = ~₹325 each, sensible.

quiz.q: Which split of Indian households is MECE?
options: Households that rent, that own, and that have a home loan
Households owning a scooter, owning a car, and owning neither
Households in big cities, in smaller towns, and in villages
Households in metros, in Tier 2 cities, and in villages
quiz.why: Each household falls in exactly one place type, so the split is exclusive and exhaustive. The metro/Tier 2/village split looks tidy but leaves out small towns, so it is not exhaustive.

quiz.q: You size gym members as 'working adults who exercise' plus 'people aged 25 to 40 who exercise'. What is wrong?
options: The groups overlap, so working adults aged 25 to 40 are counted twice
The groups are too broad, so the total will be undercounted
Age does not change gym habits, so that segment adds nothing
Two segments are too few, as MECE needs at least five buckets
quiz.why: A working 30-year-old sits in both buckets, which is double counting. Adding more buckets does not fix overlap; the cuts must be exclusive.

quiz.q: You are sizing annual school fees paid in a city. Which cut changes the answer the most?
options: By the parent's job: salaried, business, or farming income
By the child's home language: Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, or other
By whether the family owns a car or only a two-wheeler
By the child's age band: pre-primary, primary, and secondary
quiz.why: Fees differ sharply by school stage, so age is the cut that changes behaviour. Parent's job feels relevant but groups children with very different fees together, so it adds work without sharpening the number.

quiz.q: A city has 30 lakh people. Low 50% spend ₹100 a month on OTT, middle 40% spend ₹300, high 10% spend ₹800. Monthly spend?
options: ₹51 crore, by adding only the low and middle segments
₹75 crore, from 15 + 36 + 24 across the three segments
₹120 crore, using the plain average rate of ₹400 for everyone
₹7.5 crore, by slipping a factor of ten on lakh x rupees
quiz.why: Segment sizes are 15, 12 and 3 lakh, giving 15, 36 and 24 crore. Using a simple average of the three rates ignores that most people sit in the cheap segment and overstates the total.

title: Demand-side vs supply-side sizing
blurb: Count what people want, count what providers can deliver, and see if they agree.

lessons.heading: Two ways to look at a market
lessons.body: Demand-side asks how many people want the thing and how often. Supply-side asks how many providers exist and how much each can deliver. For autos in Pune, demand is riders per day; supply is autos times rides per auto.

lessons.heading: Choose by what you know
lessons.body: If you know consumers better, start with demand, for example daily commuters. If the suppliers are easy to picture, such as petrol pumps or hospitals, start with supply. Pick the side that gives fewer shaky assumptions.

lessons.heading: Supply has a capacity ceiling
lessons.body: A doctor sees only so many patients; a taxi runs only so many hours. Use capacity times utilisation, for example 70% of autos on the road. Supply-side numbers cannot exceed physical limits.

lessons.heading: Demand can exceed supply
lessons.body: If people want more than the supply serves, the real answer is the lower one for actual sales. Mention that unmet demand exists, for example surge pricing during rain in Mumbai. This shows commercial thinking.

lessons.heading: Use both to cross-check
lessons.body: Estimate one way, then the other. If they agree within 2x, you can be fairly confident. If not, one of your assumptions is off, and finding which one is the real insight.

example.prompt: How many auto-rickshaw rides happen in Pune per day?
walk: Demand side: Pune ~70 lakh people.
5% take an auto on a given day: 3.5 lakh rides.
Supply side: ~40,000 autos registered.
70% are on the road on a day: 28,000 autos.
Each makes ~12 rides: 28,000 x 12 = 3.4 lakh rides.
The two sides agree within 3%.
Answer: about 3.5 lakh rides a day.

quiz.q: Which question is easiest to size from the supply side?
options: Patients treated per year by private hospitals in Hyderabad
Cups of chai bought each day by office workers in Bengaluru
Mobile data used per day by college students in Delhi
Rides taken on the Kolkata tram in a typical month by tourists
quiz.why: Hospitals are few and countable, with beds and patients per bed as clear capacity numbers. The other three start from people's habits, where demand is the more natural entry point.

quiz.q: A city has 500 labs, each able to run 120 tests a day at 60% utilisation. Demand is 50,000 tests a day. How many tests are actually done?
options: About 50,000, because demand decides what gets done
About 60,000, because labs can run at full capacity
About 43,000, the average of the demand and supply figures
About 36,000, because supply is 500 x 120 x 0.6
quiz.why: Supply is 500 x 120 x 0.6 = 36,000, and actual tests cannot exceed it even if demand is higher. Averaging the two sides blends a real physical limit with a wish, which is a tempting but wrong shortcut.

quiz.q: Your demand-side and supply-side estimates for daily bike taxi rides differ by 10x. What is the best response?
options: Report the midpoint of the two so that neither side is ignored
Find the shakiest assumption on each side and check for a unit slip or wrong share
Trust the supply side because it uses more steps and is more detailed
Report the lower figure because it is the more conservative choice
quiz.why: A 10x gap usually means one assumption or unit is off, and finding it is the insight. Averaging or picking a side hides the error instead of locating it.

quiz.q: A city has 30,000 autos, 80% on the road, each doing 10 rides a day. How many rides per day?
options: About 3 lakh rides, counting every registered auto as active
About 24,000 rides, counting only the autos on the road
About 2.4 lakh rides, from 24,000 active autos x 10
About 24 lakh rides, from an extra zero on the lakh conversion
quiz.why: 30,000 x 0.8 = 24,000 active autos, and 24,000 x 10 = 2.4 lakh rides. Skipping the 80% utilisation step gives 3 lakh, the most tempting slip.

title: Triangulation and sanity checks
blurb: Reach the same number from two directions and compare it to a known benchmark.

lessons.heading: What triangulation is
lessons.body: You estimate the same quantity with two independent methods, for example top-down and bottom-up. If both land close, your answer gains credibility. If not, you have found where your thinking is weak.

lessons.heading: Make the methods independent
lessons.body: Two methods that share the same key assumption do not count as independent. Population-based and capacity-based routes are independent; two population-based routes are not. Aim for different starting points.

lessons.heading: Use known benchmarks
lessons.body: Compare against anything you know: a metro line's ridership, India's total petrol use, a city's number of schools. A quick ratio check such as 'that is 1 in 6 people' also works. Benchmarks catch order-of-magnitude slips fast.

lessons.heading: Per-capita checks
lessons.body: Divide your total by population. A result of ₹50 lakh per person per year for tea is absurd; ₹1,500 is plausible. Per-household and per-day checks catch the most errors.

lessons.heading: What to do when numbers disagree
lessons.body: List the assumptions in each route and find the biggest lever. Adjust the least certain one and recompute. Say aloud which you trust more and why, then settle on one rounded number.

example.prompt: How many people use the Delhi Metro on a weekday?
walk: Top-down: NCR population ~3 crore.
About 12% ride the metro on a weekday: 36 lakh.
Bottom-up: ~250 stations.
Average ~15,000 entries a day per station: 37.5 lakh.
Two methods: 36 lakh and 37.5 lakh, within 5%.
Per capita check: 1 in 8 people, plausible for a big metro network.
Answer: roughly 35 to 40 lakh trips a day.

quiz.q: Which pair gives a truly independent triangulation of annual LPG cylinder use?
options: Households x cylinders each, versus population x cylinders per person
Households x cylinders each, versus distributors x cylinders delivered
Urban households x urban use, versus rural households x rural use
Population x LPG share, versus population x daily-cooking share
quiz.why: One route starts from consumers and the other from suppliers, so errors in one are unlikely to repeat in the other. The other pairs share a population base or are just one route split in two.

quiz.q: Your model gives ₹40,000 crore a year of mobile recharge for a city of 50 lakh people. What does a per-capita check say?
options: About ₹8,000 per person, which is high but plausible for a metro
About ₹80,000 per person, plausible once business SIMs are included
About ₹80,000 per person, far too high, so look for a large slip
About ₹800 per person, which is low for a city this size
quiz.why: ₹40,000 crore / 50 lakh = ₹80,000 each, many times a realistic yearly spend of a few thousand rupees. Explaining it away with business SIMs rationalises an order-of-magnitude error.

quiz.q: Top-down gives 36 lakh and bottom-up gives 3.6 crore riders. What is the best next step?
options: Compare the assumptions in both routes for a lakh versus crore slip
Take the geometric mean of the two and report about 1.1 crore
Add a third route built on the same population share and go with the majority
Report 36 lakh since the top-down route is usually more reliable
quiz.why: A clean 10x gap points to a unit or share slip, which a line-by-line comparison finds. A third route sharing the same assumption is not independent, so it only repeats the original mistake.

quiz.q: Your estimate says 40 lakh people use the Delhi Metro on a weekday. Which check is the most informative?
options: Check it is below NCR's 3 crore population, so it is possible
Check it is higher than the count of stations, about 250
Check that it is a round number so it is easy to state aloud
Compare it with Mumbai suburban rail's 70 lakh daily riders
quiz.why: A comparable known system gives a real scale to test against. Being under the whole population or above the station count passes even for estimates that are badly wrong.

title: Penetration, frequency and price models
blurb: Market size = users x how often x how much each time.

lessons.heading: The three-factor engine
lessons.body: Many market questions fit: addressable people x penetration x frequency x price. Penetration is the share who use it, frequency is how often, price is rupees per use. Each factor is easy to reason about separately.

lessons.heading: Penetration needs a funnel
lessons.body: Start with all people, narrow to those who could use it (urban, smartphone, adult), then those who actually do. Keep each step a clean percentage. Mention adoption curves if the product is new.

lessons.heading: Frequency is usually the biggest lever
lessons.body: Weekly versus monthly use changes the answer by 4x. Sense-check with your own behaviour and a typical friend's. Split heavy and light users when behaviour is very uneven.

lessons.heading: Price is an average, not a menu price
lessons.body: Use the realised average after discounts and cheaper variants. A ₹400 average order might mix ₹150 snacks and ₹800 family orders. Say what you assume the mix to be.

lessons.heading: Convert at the end
lessons.body: Orders per user per month x 12 gives annual. Then multiply by users and price, and convert to crore. Write units on each line so you never multiply orders by households by accident.

example.prompt: Annual online food delivery market in India in ₹.
walk: Population: 145 crore, urban ~35%: ~50 crore.
Penetration: 8% of urban people order online: 4 crore users.
Frequency: 2 orders a month = 24 a year.
Orders: 4 crore x 24 = 96 crore a year.
Price: ~₹400 average order value.
Market: 96 crore x 400 = about ₹38,400 crore.
Round: about ₹38,000 crore a year. Sanity: ~₹1,000 per urban person a year, plausible.

quiz.q: Which formula best fits 'annual market in rupees for packaged tea in India'?
options: Households x share buying packaged tea x price per kg
Households x kg bought per year x price per cup of tea
Population x share buying tea x kg per household x price per kg
Households x share buying tea x kg per year x price per kg
quiz.why: It chains the base, penetration, frequency (quantity) and price with matching units. Dropping quantity or mixing kg with a per-cup price breaks the units.

quiz.q: For online food delivery you are unsure whether the typical user orders weekly or monthly, and whether the average order is ₹350 or ₹400. Which matters more?
options: Price, because it is multiplied directly into the revenue figure
Frequency, as weekly versus monthly is a 4x gap and price differs by about 15%
Penetration, because every later step depends on that first percentage
Both equally, because all the factors multiply into the answer
quiz.why: Every factor multiplies, but the size of the uncertainty is what matters, and frequency swings 4x here. 'All factors multiply' is true yet ignores that one range is much wider.

quiz.q: 2 crore users order 3 times a month at ₹300 an order. What is the annual market?
options: About ₹1,800 crore, forgetting to convert months to a year
About ₹2,160 crore, the right digits but ten times too small
About ₹21,600 crore, from 72 crore orders at ₹300 each
About ₹2.16 lakh crore, off by a factor of a hundred
quiz.why: 2 crore x 36 orders = 72 crore orders, times ₹300 is ₹21,600 crore. Stopping at one month gives ₹1,800 crore, the most common slip.

quiz.q: Of 4 crore users, 20% order about 10 times a month and the other 80% about once. Monthly orders?
options: About 11.2 crore, from 8 crore plus 3.2 crore
About 22 crore, using the simple average of 5.5 orders each
About 8 crore, counting only the heavy users
About 40 crore, treating every user as a heavy user
quiz.why: Heavy users give 0.8 crore x 10 = 8 crore and light users give 3.2 crore x 1 = 3.2 crore. Averaging 10 and 1 gives 5.5, which ignores that most users are light.

title: Hard mixed cases and presenting under pressure
blurb: Combine methods, keep calm and deliver a crisp, defended number.

lessons.heading: Mix the methods
lessons.body: Hard cases combine segmentation, rates and cross-checks. For Indian weddings you might use birth cohorts for count, spend bands for value and a per-household check. Name each block aloud as you move between them.

lessons.heading: Time-box yourself
lessons.body: You get a few minutes. Spend roughly 20% on clarifying and structure, 60% on calculation and 20% on sanity check and conclusion. If stuck on one assumption, state a placeholder and move on.

lessons.heading: Handle a challenge calmly
lessons.body: When the interviewer asks 'why 30%?', give the reason in one sentence and say what would change it. Offer to run a quick sensitivity: 'If it is 20%, the answer drops by a third.' That shows command of the model.

lessons.heading: Stay on one page
lessons.body: Keep structure, assumptions and final number visible on one page. Number your assumptions. If asked to revisit, you can point to the exact line instead of redoing everything.

lessons.heading: Close with a number and a caveat
lessons.body: Finish with 'So roughly ₹9 lakh crore a year, and the biggest sensitivity is the share of high-spend weddings.' One number, one check, one sensitivity. Then stop talking.

example.prompt: How big is the Indian wedding market per year in ₹?
walk: Approach: number of weddings x average spend, segmented by budget.
Each birth cohort is ~2.3 crore; ~90% marry: about 2 crore people.
That is about 1 crore weddings a year.
Segments: 70% at ₹3 lakh, 25% at ₹15 lakh, 5% at ₹60 lakh.
Average: 2.1 + 3.75 + 3 = ₹8.85 lakh, about ₹9 lakh.
Market: 1 crore x ₹9 lakh = ₹9 lakh crore.
Check: about 1 wedding per 30 households a year, roughly ₹3,000 per household per year on average. Biggest lever: share and spend of the top 5% segment.

quiz.q: The interviewer asks why you assumed 5% of weddings are high-spend. What is the best reply?
options: Cite it as a known industry figure so that you sound confident
Admit it is a guess and ask the interviewer for the right figure
Give one reason, say what would change it, offer a sensitivity
Rebuild the model with a new split to show that you can adapt
quiz.why: A one-line reason plus a sensitivity shows command of the model. Citing an invented source or abandoning the assumption both lose credibility.

quiz.q: In a 10-minute case, how should you split the time between structure, calculation and the final check?
options: 2 minutes for structure, 6 for calculation, 2 for the check
4 minutes for structure, 5 for calculation, 1 for the sanity check
1 minute for structure, 6 for calculation, 3 for the sanity check
3 minutes for structure, 3 for calculation, 4 for the sanity check
quiz.why: A 20/60/20 split gives 2, 6 and 2 minutes. Spending extra time on structure feels safe but squeezes the calculation and the check.

quiz.q: Weddings split 60% at ₹4 lakh, 30% at ₹12 lakh and 10% at ₹50 lakh. With 1 crore weddings a year, what is the market?
options: About ₹1.1 lakh crore, with a factor of ten lost in the units
About ₹11 lakh crore, using a weighted average of ₹11 lakh
About ₹22 lakh crore, using the plain average of the three spends
About ₹110 lakh crore, with a factor of ten added in the units
quiz.why: The weighted average is 2.4 + 3.6 + 5 = ₹11 lakh, and 1 crore x ₹11 lakh = ₹11 lakh crore. A plain average of the three spends ignores that most weddings are cheap.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to close a wedding market estimate?
options: Give a wide range of ₹5 to ₹15 lakh crore to stay safe
Recap every assumption in order and then give the number
State the number and list three or four caveats to be thorough
State one number and name the sensitivity that matters most
quiz.why: One number plus one sensitivity is crisp and shows you know the key lever. A wide range or a long list of caveats dilutes the message and invites doubt.
